characterList.description: A dimeric protein, depicted in shades of red and pink, embedded within the cell membrane with a large extracellular domain and transmembrane domain.
characterList.name: mGluR GPCR

characterList.description: A heterotrimeric protein complex in shades of orange and light red, connected to the intracellular side of the mGluR GPCR.
characterList.name: G Protein

characterList.description: A light green protein responsible for phosphorylating the C-terminus of the mGluR GPCR.
characterList.name: GRK (G protein-coupled Receptor Kinase)

characterList.description: A magenta protein that binds to the mGluR GPCR after phosphorylation.
characterList.name: Arrestin

characterList.description: A gray cage-like structure that engulfs the GPCR for receptor endocytosis.
characterList.name: Clathrin-coated Pit/Vesicle

content_metadata.description: This video explores the diffusion behavior of the mGluR GPCR within the cell membrane and its functional cycle of activation, regulation, and endocytosis.

qAndA.answer: Directed Brownian, Normal Brownian, and Confinement Restriction.
qAndA.question: What are the three different modes of diffusion shown in the video?

qAndA.answer: It dissociates into its alpha and beta-gamma subunits.
qAndA.question: What happens to the G protein after the mGluR GPCR is activated?

qAndA.answer: They phosphorylate the C-terminus of the activated GPCR.
qAndA.question: What is the role of GRKs?

qAndA.answer: Binding of Arrestin to the phosphorylated C-terminus.
qAndA.question: What causes the mGluR GPCR to become immobilized?

qAndA.answer: It is endocytosed into the cell within clathrin-coated vesicles, where it can be degraded or recycled.
qAndA.question: What is the final fate of the mGluR GPCR?

timecoded_text_to_speech.text: Cell membranes are incredibly crowded environments packed with proteins, lipids and carbohydrates.
Competition for space is fierce and membrane proteins have to contend with many other molecules,
as well as macromolecular structures from within, above and below the phospholipid bilayer.
Metavitropic glutamate receptors are class C, G-protein coupled receptor membrane proteins,
or GPCRs, as they are commonly known.
They have an extracellular domain with ligand binding regions, and a transmembrane domain
with intracellular C-termini.
Previously, it was believed that membrane proteins, such as GPCRs, will,
more often than not, exhibit random brownie emotion when diffusing laterally across the membrane,
as pictured here.
We now know that this is seldom the case, due to frequent interactions with other proteins,
lipids, as well as larger macromolecular structures and organelles.
In fact, GPCRs can exhibit as many as four different modes of diffusion,
where mobility can be influenced by interactions with other molecules and structures
either above, within, or beneath the cell membrane.
Yanagawa et al observed that metavitropic glutamate receptor-free,
pre-coupled with G-proteins, will diffuse rapidly across the membrane,
exhibiting either brownie or directed motion.
After the GPCR molecule transitions from fast to much lower displacement,
confinement can be observed.
This takes place within fences or corrals, principally formed by the intracellular actin-based cytoskeleton,
but also with a high degree of molecular crowding, including an increased concentration of cholesterol.
Agonis binding promotes a conformational change in the GPCR, from the resting to the active state.
In the active state, Englua is more likely to exhibit confinement within cytoskeletal fences,
which form a hot spot for G-protein activation.
The activated G-protein dissociates into its alpha and beta-gammer subunits.
Still within the actin cytoskeletal fences, the C-terminus of the GPCR becomes phosphorylated
by G-protein-coupled receptor kinases.
C-terminal phosphorylation acts as a signal for the recruitment of a rest in to the metavitropic glutamate receptor.
A rest in binding causes the GPCR to become immobilized within a claffer-encoded pit,
where the diffusion mode transitions from confinement to restriction.
After immobilization, the GPCR is endocytosed into the cell within claffer-encoded vesicles,
where it can be degraded or recycled for future use.
In the active state, the C-terminus of the GPCR is the most likely to be degraded.

youtube_description:
Metabotropic glutamate receptors are class C GPCRs, their lateral cis-membrane diffusion, like all membrane proteins, is influenced by their binding interactions with small molecules, other proteins, and larger macromolecular complexes.

This animation features single molecule tracking data from Yanagawa et al (2018) https://doi.org/10.1126/scisignal.aao1917
